title: Baruch
subtitle: a confession, a poem on wisdom, a mother's comfort, and a letter against idols
lead: Baruch is a short book in the Greek Bible set among the Jews exiled to Babylon. It claims to be written by Baruch, the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah. It has a prose frame (1:1-14), a long confession of sin (1:15-3:8), a poem in praise of wisdom given to Israel as the Law (3:9-4:4), and a poem in which Jerusalem speaks as a mother to her children and is comforted (4:5-5:9). Chapter 6, the Letter of Jeremiah, is a separate short work against the idols of Babylon, printed as Baruch 6 in Catholic Bibles and the KJV.
Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah; they are not in the Jewish Bible, and Protestants place them among the Apocrypha.
facts: Catholic and Orthodox churches; among the Apocrypha for Protestants; not in the Jewish Bible
6 chapters, 213 verses (chapter 6 is the Letter of Jeremiah)

audience.to: Jews living under foreign rule, in Judea and in the dispersion.
audience.why: To lead them to confess their sins, seek wisdom in the Law, hope for the return of the scattered, and refuse the worship of idols.

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah as its chapter 6, among the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Orthodox churches read Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah, as two books, after Jeremiah in the Greek Old Testament.

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place Baruch and the Letter among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read Baruch as a collection of pieces by different hands written after the exile, and the Letter as an earlier Jewish tract against idols.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Neither work is in the Jewish Bible; both are windows on Jewish prayer and polemic in the centuries before Jesus.

canon.summary: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah. Protestants place them among the Apocrypha, and they are not in the Jewish Bible.
